title: ICSE Class 10 History, Chapter 2: Growth of Nationalism, Step by Step
subtitle: For students who find history hard. Economic exploitation, Lord Lytton's repressive policies and the Ilbert Bill, Rammohan Roy and Jyotiba Phule, the press, the early associations and the birth of the Indian National Congress, all held together by one idea (pain, voice and platform), in small steps with model answers, quick checks, an exam toolkit and a last-minute revision sheet. Follows the ICSE Class 10 syllabus, Chapter 2 (Growth of Nationalism), in the order of Total History & Civics.

changelog.text: First version: the whole chapter in small steps, with model answers, quick checks, a last-minute revision sheet, a self-test and a section for teachers and parents.

children.label: How to use this roadmap
children.desc:
- Go in order. Each step is small. The **numbers** on the map show the order, and the **Next** button at the bottom of each box takes you to the next step.
- Click a box to open it. Read the idea and the model answer, then do **Your turn**.
- **Every answer is a point plus one fact:** a name, a date or a place. One point earns one mark.
- Write your answer in your notebook **before** you open the answer box.
- Got it wrong? That is fine. Read the answer, then try the next one.
- Each milestone ends with a **Quick check**. Click an answer: it tells you if you are right, and why.
- When a step feels easy, mark it **Done**. Your progress is saved on this device.

**One idea runs through this whole chapter: pain, voice and platform.** British rule caused **common pain** (exploitation and harsh laws). **Reformers and the press** gave Indians a **voice**. Associations, then the **Congress (1885)**, gave them a **platform**.

children.label: About this roadmap
children.desc:
**What it is.** A step-by-step path through Chapter 2, *Growth of Nationalism*, of the History part of the ICSE Class 10 History and Civics syllabus. It follows the order of *Total History & Civics* for Class 10.

**Who it is for.** Class 10 students who find history hard, and want to understand this chapter and score decent marks in it. It also works for revision, and for the teachers and parents helping them: the last milestone is written for adults.

**The one idea.** Nationalism grew from pain, voice and platform. British rule caused common pain through exploitation and harsh laws. Reformers and the press gave Indians a voice. Associations, and then the Congress in 1885, gave them a platform.

**How it is different from the textbook.** The textbook gives long lists of factors, reformers and associations. Here they hang on one idea, **pain, voice and platform**, and every answer is taught as **a point plus one fact**, with fresh model answers. Two textbook slips are flagged gently: the year sati was banned, and what happened to the Ilbert Bill.

**What is inside.**
- 11 milestones and 46 small steps. The 38 solid steps are the core path. The dashed ones are optional.
- 44 practice questions with hidden answers.
- 28 click-to-check questions that say right or wrong, and why: a quick check after each of the 6 main milestones, and a 10-question self-test.
- A **last-minute revision sheet**: every date, key term, name and trap on one page.
- *Start here* fixes the basic skills the chapter needs, and *Check yourself* shows which ones to work on.
- Optional: picture study and two structured challenge questions, and a section for teachers and parents with a 6-period lesson plan, the mistakes to watch for and a 5-minute exit ticket.

**Can you trust it?** Dates, names and places follow the textbook, and the few slips found in it are pointed out gently. A computer program checks that every date sits in the right order and every click-to-check answer is marked right. All the model answers are written fresh, so students still get fresh practice from their textbook. If you spot a mistake, use **Report a problem** at the top of the page.

**Not official.** This is a free, independent resource. It follows the ICSE syllabus but is not made or endorsed by CISCE or by any publisher. It is shared under the **CC BY-SA 4.0** licence: you may copy, adapt and share it, as long as you credit it and share your version the same way.

children.label: Check yourself (2 minutes)
children.desc: Four quick questions. Write your answers first, then open each box. If you get one wrong, do the step named in the answer.

faq.q: 1. What does 'nationalism' mean?
faq.a: A feeling of **oneness**: people see themselves as **one nation**. Wrong? Do *What nationalism means*.

faq.q: 2. Before the British, were Indians loyal to India or to their king?
faq.a: Mostly to **their own king**. Wrong? Do *Why India was not one nation before*.

faq.q: 3. Is a harsh British law 'pain', 'voice' or 'platform'?
faq.a: **Pain.** Wrong? Do *Pain, voice and platform*.

faq.q: 4. A 2-mark question asks for two factors. What do you write?
faq.a: **Two points**, each with **one fact**. Wrong? Do *How ICSE asks, and the answer shape*.

children.label: Who's who in this chapter
children.desc:
Learn these names first. They come up again and again.

- **Viceroy:** the British ruler of India. Three matter here: **Lord Lytton** (harsh laws), **Lord Ripon** (kinder), **Lord Dufferin** (when the Congress began).
- **Reformers:** **Raja Rammohan Roy** (Bengal) and **Jyotiba Phule** (Maharashtra).
- **Early leaders:** **Dadabhai Naoroji**, **Surendranath Banerjee**, **W.C. Bonnerjee**.
- **A.O. Hume:** a retired British official who helped found the **Congress**.
- **Vernacular:** in an **Indian language** (Bengali, Marathi, Hindi...).

faq.q: Your turn: which Viceroy is linked with harsh laws in 1878?
faq.a: **Lord Lytton.**

children.label: Pain, voice and platform
children.desc:
This chapter has **one shape**. Nationalism grew in three stages.

- **Pain:** British rule hurt **every class** of Indians (economic exploitation) and passed **harsh laws** (repressive policies).
- **Voice:** **reformers** and the **press** taught Indians to think, question and speak up.
- **Platform:** **associations** brought people together, and in 1885 the **Congress** gave all India one platform.

The syllabus lists four factors: **economic exploitation, repressive policies, reform movements and the press**. Pain gives you the first two; voice gives you the last two.

faq.q: Your turn: the Vernacular Press Act. Pain, voice or platform?
faq.a: **Pain**: it was a **repressive** law. (It attacked the press, which was the voice.)

children.label: How ICSE asks, and the answer shape
children.desc:
ICSE asks history in three ways.

- **Multiple choice:** 1 mark. Pick one option.
- **Short answer:** usually 2 marks. Write **two points**.
- **Structured question:** parts (a), (b), (c), worth 3 or 4 marks each. Write **one point per mark**.

Each point has **one fact**: a name, a date or a place. A point without a fact looks vague and loses marks.

**Model answer.** *State two factors that led to the growth of nationalism.*

- **Economic exploitation:** peasants paid heavy **land revenue** and artisans lost work to British goods.
- **Repressive policies:** **Lord Lytton's** Vernacular Press Act (1878) gagged Indian newspapers.

faq.q: Your turn: what is wrong with this answer? 'The British were harsh to Indians.'
faq.a: It has **no fact**. Add one: for example, *'Lord Lytton passed the Vernacular Press Act in 1878.'*

topics.label: What nationalism is, and why it grew
topics.desc:
**Goal:** say what nationalism means, and why it grew so late in India.

Practice: in the chapter exercises in *Total History & Civics*, Exercise I (short answers) on the meaning of nationalism and why it was lacking.

children.label: What nationalism means
children.desc:
**Nationalism** is a feeling of **oneness**. People who share a land, a history and a culture start to see themselves as **one nation**.

- It is like a class becoming a **team**. Before, each student cared only about themselves. Now they say 'we'.
- In India, this feeling grew in the **second half of the 1800s**.
- It led to the **Indian National Congress** in **1885**.

faq.q: Your turn: explain 'nationalism' in one sentence.
faq.a: A feeling of **oneness** among people who share a land, history and culture, and see themselves as **one nation**.

children.label: Why India was not one nation before
children.desc:
India is very old. But for most of its history it was **many kingdoms**.

- Sometimes one empire ruled a large part. Still, people were loyal to **their own king or kingdom**, not to India.
- Resistance to the British was **local and scattered**, led by old rulers, zamindars and ex-soldiers.
- **1857** failed, but it **inspired** Indians to fight foreign rule together.

Strangely, it was **British rule itself** that made Indians feel like one people. Everyone suffered from the **same ruler**.

faq.q: Your turn: why was the feeling of nationalism missing before the British?
faq.a: India was divided into **many kingdoms**, and people's loyalty was to **their own king**, not to India as a whole.

children.label: From loyalty to a king to loyalty to India
children.desc:
Think of the change as **who you belong to**.

- **Before:** 'I am the subject of the Raja of my state.'
- **After:** 'I am an **Indian**, and India is being harmed.'

Three things made this change happen under British rule:
- **one ruler** over all of India, harming all alike;
- **Western education**, which brought ideas of **liberty and equality**;
- the memory of **1857**, which showed resistance was possible.

faq.q: Your turn: give two reasons why nationalism grew in the late 1800s.
faq.a: **Economic exploitation** by the British hurt every class. **Reformers and the press** spread new ideas of liberty and equality.

children.label: Quick check: what nationalism is
children.desc:
Three questions on this milestone. Click an answer to check it.

Wrong? Read the reason, then look back at the step it names.

quiz.q: What is nationalism?
options: A law passed by the British
Loyalty to one king or kingdom
Belief in one religion for everyone
A feeling of oneness among people who see themselves as one nation
quiz.why: It is a shared feeling of **oneness**. Loyalty to a king is exactly what India had **before**. See *What nationalism means*.

quiz.q: Before British rule, people in India were mostly loyal to:
quiz.why: India was many **kingdoms**. See *Why India was not one nation before*.

quiz.q: Which earlier event first inspired Indians to fight foreign rule together?
quiz.why: 1857 failed, but it **inspired** later struggle. See *Why India was not one nation before*.

topics.label: Pain 1: economic exploitation
topics.desc:
**Goal:** explain how British economic policy hurt every class of Indians. The textbook calls this **the most important** factor.

Practice: in the chapter exercises in *Total History & Civics*, Exercise I (short answers) on economic exploitation and industrial stagnation, and Exercise II (structured) question 1.

children.label: Peasants and artisans
children.desc:
British policy served **Britain**, not India.

- **Peasants:** the main victims. Huge **land revenue** and taxes pushed them into the hands of **landlords and moneylenders**.
- **Artisans and craftsmen:** British power was used to destroy Indian **handicrafts**. India became a **source of raw materials** and a **market** for British goods.

**Model answer.** *Give two examples of British economic exploitation.*

- Peasants paid very high **land revenue**, which pushed them into **debt**.
- India supplied **raw materials** cheaply and had to buy British **finished goods**, which ruined Indian **handicrafts**.

faq.q: Your turn: why did Indian industry not grow under the British? Two points.
faq.a: Indian handicrafts were **destroyed** by cheap British goods. India was kept as a **raw-material supplier and market**, not a maker.

children.label: Workers and the educated
children.desc:
- **The working class:** new **factories** created workers. They were exploited by factory owners, mostly **Englishmen**. They were few, but their outlook covered **all India**.
- **The educated Indians:** the only good job was **government service**. Competition was high and promotion was **bleak**. They had hoped Britain would build up India. Instead it kept India **backward**.

**The result:** every class felt the problem was **British rule**. To fight it, they had to come together on **one national platform**.

faq.q: Your turn: why were educated Indians unhappy with British rule?
faq.a: Their only job was **government service**, where the top posts were closed to them, and British policy kept India **economically backward**.

children.label: Quick check: economic exploitation
children.desc:
Three questions on this milestone. Click an answer to check it.

Wrong? Read the reason, then look back at the step it names.

quiz.q: Who were the main victims of British economic policy?
options: The zamindars who supported the British
quiz.why: Peasants paid **huge land revenue** and fell into debt. See *Peasants and artisans*.

quiz.q: What did India become for British industry?
options: A source of raw materials and a market for finished goods
A buyer of raw materials from Britain
quiz.why: Raw materials **out**, finished goods **in**. See *Peasants and artisans*.

quiz.q: Why were educated Indians unhappy?
options: They were not allowed to read English
They had to pay land revenue
Government jobs were few and promotion was bleak
They were sent to work in factories
quiz.why: Their only hope was **government service**, and it was closed to them at the top. See *Workers and the educated*.

topics.label: Pain 2: repressive policies
topics.desc:
**Goal:** explain Lord Lytton's harsh measures (1877 to 1880) and the Ilbert Bill row (1883).

Practice: in the chapter exercises in *Total History & Civics*, Exercise I (short answers) on the Vernacular Press Act and the Ilbert Bill, and Exercise II question 2.

children.label: Lord Lytton's Durbar
children.desc:
**Lord Lytton** was Viceroy from 1876 to 1880. His rule **sped up** nationalism.

In **1877** he held a grand **Delhi Durbar** to proclaim **Queen Victoria** the **Empress of India**.

- **Lakhs of rupees** were spent on the show.
- At the same time, people were dying in a terrible **famine**.
- Nothing was done for them. Indians felt **insulted**.

faq.q: Your turn: why did the Delhi Durbar anger Indians?
faq.a: Lakhs were spent on a **show** for Queen Victoria in 1877, while people were dying in a **famine**.

children.label: Two laws of 1878: the Press Act and the Arms Act
children.desc:
- **Vernacular Press Act (1878):** newspapers in **Indian languages** could not print anything that stirred **dislike** of the government. **English** papers were **not** covered. **Lord Ripon** repealed it in **1882**.
- **Indian Arms Act (1878):** an Indian needed a **licence** to keep arms. It did not apply to the **British**.

Both laws treated Indians as **suspects** in their own country.

**Model answer.** *Who passed the Vernacular Press Act, and why?*

- **Lord Lytton** passed it in 1878.
- He wanted to **silence** Indian-language newspapers that criticised the government.

faq.q: Your turn: why was the Arms Act seen as unfair?
faq.a: It needed a **licence** for Indians to keep arms, but **not for the British**: it was **racial**.

children.label: Lytton's other blows: the ICS age and cotton duties
children.desc:
- **ICS age cut:** the top age for the **Indian Civil Service** exam was cut from **21 to 19**. The exam was in **London**, so few Indians could manage it so young.
- **Cotton duties removed:** the tax on **British cloth** entering India was dropped. It helped British mills and **hurt Indian industry**.

faq.q: Your turn: why did cutting the ICS age to 19 hurt Indians?
faq.a: The exam was held in **London**. Young Indians could hardly prepare and travel there by **19**, so fewer Indians could get in.

children.label: The Ilbert Bill: can an Indian judge try a European?
children.desc:
In **1883**, under **Lord Ripon**, **C.P. Ilbert** brought a bill. It said **Indian judges** could **try Europeans**, just like British judges.

- Europeans in India were furious. They formed a **Defence Association** to protect their privileges.
- The government **backed down**. (Your textbook says the bill was withdrawn; really it was passed in a much weaker form.)
- Educated Indians learned a lesson: **no justice** could be expected when **European interests** were involved.
- They saw that **organised protest works**: the Europeans had just shown how.

faq.q: Your turn: what was the Ilbert Bill, and why did it fail?
faq.a: It let **Indian judges try Europeans**. Europeans **protested** fiercely, and the government **backed down**.

children.label: Quick check: repressive policies
children.desc:
Three questions on this milestone. Click an answer to check it.

Wrong? Read the reason, then look back at the step it names.

quiz.q: Who passed the Vernacular Press Act?
quiz.why: **Lytton** passed it in 1878; **Ripon** repealed it in 1882. See *Two laws of 1878: the Press Act and the Arms Act*.

quiz.q: What did the Ilbert Bill propose?
options: That the ICS age be cut to 19
That Queen Victoria be Empress of India
That Indian judges could try Europeans
That Indians could not carry arms
quiz.why: Equal powers for **Indian judges**. Europeans protested and it was **watered down**. See *The Ilbert Bill: can an Indian judge try a European?*.

quiz.q: The Delhi Durbar of 1877 angered Indians because:
options: it made Indians pay a new salt tax
lakhs were spent on it while people were dying in a famine
quiz.why: Pomp during a **famine**. See *Lord Lytton's Durbar*.

topics.label: Voice 1: Rammohan Roy and Jyotiba Phule
topics.desc:
**Goal:** explain how two reformers prepared the ground for nationalism.

Practice: in the chapter exercises in *Total History & Civics*, Exercise I (short answers) on the reformers and Phule's organisation, and Exercise III (picture study).

children.label: Raja Rammohan Roy: one God, no sati
children.desc:
**Raja Rammohan Roy** studied Sanskrit, Persian, Arabic and English. He wanted India to take **the best of East and West**.

- **Religion:** he believed in **one God** and opposed **idol worship**. In **1828** he founded the **Brahmo Sabha**, later the **Brahmo Samaj**.
- **Society:** he campaigned against **sati**, purdah, polygamy and child marriage. **Lord William Bentinck** banned sati in **1829**. (Your textbook prints 1820; the law came in 1829.)
- **Women:** he wanted women to have a right to **inheritance and property**.

He is called the **father of the Indian Renaissance**.

faq.q: Your turn: name the society Rammohan Roy founded, and two of its beliefs.
faq.a: The **Brahmo Samaj**. It believed in **one God** and **opposed idol worship**.

children.label: Rammohan Roy the journalist and nationalist
children.desc:
Roy was also a **pioneer of Indian journalism**.

- He brought out journals in Bengali, English, Hindi and Persian, like the Bengali weekly ***Samvad Kaumudi*** and the Persian ***Mirat-ul-Akhbar***.
- He began **public agitation** for rights. He asked for **equality** between Indians and Europeans in courts, **trial by jury**, and **Indians in high posts**.

So he showed Indians how to **speak up**: the first step to a national movement.

faq.q: Your turn: give two ways Rammohan Roy helped the national movement.
faq.a: He started **newspapers** like *Samvad Kaumudi* to spread ideas. He **demanded rights** for Indians, like judicial equality with Europeans.

children.label: Jyotiba Phule: education and equality
children.desc:
**Jyotiba Phule** was born in a so-called **low caste** in Maharashtra. He fought for those at the bottom.

- **Women:** with his wife **Savitribai Phule** he started some of the first **schools for girls** in **Pune**. He backed **widow remarriage**.
- **Lower castes:** he opened a **school for untouchables**. His book ***Ghulamgiri*** ('slavery') compared caste to slavery.
- **Satya Shodhak Samaj (1873):** he founded it to win **social justice** for the weaker sections.

faq.q: Your turn: name the organisation Phule founded, and its aim.
faq.a: The **Satya Shodhak Samaj** (1873). It aimed at **social justice** for the **lower castes** and weaker sections.

children.label: How reform built nationalism
children.desc:
The reformers were not fighting the British directly. But they **prepared the ground**.

- They attacked **caste and untouchability**. Ideas of **equality** drew in the lower castes.
- They raised the status of **women**.
- Reformers like **Dayanand Saraswati** and **Vivekananda** gave Indians **pride** in their culture.
- They built the idea of **one society**, without privileges of caste or creed.

faq.q: Your turn: how did reform movements act as pioneers of nationalism? Two points.
faq.a: They fought **caste and untouchability**, so people saw each other as **equals**. They gave Indians **pride** in their own culture.

children.label: Quick check: the reformers
children.desc:
Three questions on this milestone. Click an answer to check it.

Wrong? Read the reason, then look back at the step it names.

quiz.q: Which society did Raja Rammohan Roy found?
quiz.why: Arya Samaj was **Dayanand Saraswati**; Satya Shodhak Samaj was **Phule**. See *Raja Rammohan Roy: one God, no sati*.

quiz.q: Jyotiba Phule's book Ghulamgiri was about:
options: the suffering of the lower castes
quiz.why: *Ghulamgiri* means **slavery**: he compared caste to it. See *Jyotiba Phule: education and equality*.

quiz.q: How did the reform movements help nationalism?
options: They taught equality and pride in Indian culture
They asked Indians to obey the British
They started the Indian National Congress
quiz.why: Equality and **pride** brought people together. See *How reform built nationalism*.

topics.label: Voice 2: the press
topics.desc:
**Goal:** explain how newspapers spread national feeling.

Practice: in the chapter exercises in *Total History & Civics*, Exercise I (short answers) on the press and important newspapers, and Exercise II question 1.

children.label: Newspapers that woke India
children.desc:
Many newspapers began in the **second half of the 1800s**:

- in English: the ***Amrita Bazar Patrika***, ***The Bengalee***, ***The Tribune***, ***The Hindu***;
- and many more in **Indian languages**.

This is exactly why Lytton's **Vernacular Press Act** went after Indian-language papers: they reached **ordinary people**.

faq.q: Your turn: name two 19th-century newspapers that spread national feeling.
faq.a: For example, the ***Amrita Bazar Patrika*** and ***The Hindu***.

children.label: Four ways the press built nationalism
children.desc:
- **Spread ideas:** patriotism, **liberty, equality** and **self-rule** reached ordinary people.
- **Criticised the government:** daily attacks on **unjust policies** exposed British rule.
- **Linked regions:** people in different parts of India **shared views** and organised together.
- **Opened a window to the world:** Indians learned what was happening abroad.

**Model answer.** *What role did the press play in the national movement?*

- It **criticised** British policies daily and exposed the true nature of British rule.
- It helped people from **different regions** share views and organise movements.

faq.q: Your turn: give one way the press made Indians feel like one people.
faq.a: It let people in **different regions** exchange views, so they felt they shared **one cause**.

children.label: Quick check: the press
children.desc:
Three questions on this milestone. Click an answer to check it.

Wrong? Read the reason, then look back at the step it names.

quiz.q: Which of these was a 19th-century nationalist newspaper?
quiz.why: The others are **later** papers (Gandhi's and Nehru's). See *Newspapers that woke India*.

quiz.q: Which is a way the press built nationalism?
options: It was printed only in London
It was controlled by the Viceroy
It criticised unjust British policies every day
quiz.why: Daily **criticism** exposed British rule. See *Four ways the press built nationalism*.

quiz.q: Which act tried to control newspapers in Indian languages?
quiz.why: 'Vernacular' means **Indian languages**. English papers were free of it. See *Two laws of 1878: the Press Act and the Arms Act*.

topics.label: Platform: associations and the birth of the Congress
topics.desc:
**Goal:** trace how local associations led to the **Indian National Congress** in 1885, and its first aims.

Practice: in the chapter exercises in *Total History & Civics*, Exercise I (short answers) on the associations and the founding of the Congress, Exercise II questions 2 and 3.

children.label: From local societies to all-India ones
children.desc:
Political associations grew step by step.

- **1838:** the **Landholders' Society**, Calcutta: the **first** political association.
- Others followed: the British Indian Association, the **Poona Sarvajanik Sabha**, and more.

Most were **local**: one city or region. But their aims were **common** to all Indians, not one religion or class. They were the **forerunners** of the Congress.

faq.q: Your turn: what was the nature of associations before the Congress?
faq.a: They were **local or regional**, but worked for **common goals** of all Indians, not one religion or class.

children.label: East India Association: Dadabhai Naoroji in London
children.desc:
**Dadabhai Naoroji** founded the **East India Association** in **London** in **1866**.

- It told **British citizens and Members of Parliament** about India's problems.
- Naoroji believed the British were basically **just**. If they knew the truth, they would **help**.
- It had branches in **Bombay, Calcutta and Madras**.

Naoroji is called the **Grand Old Man of India**.

faq.q: Your turn: which association is linked to Dadabhai Naoroji, and where was it?
faq.a: The **East India Association**, founded in **London** in 1866.

children.label: Indian Association: Surendranath Banerjee

faq.q: Your turn: give two aims of the Indian Association.
faq.a: To build **strong public opinion**, and to unite Indians on **common political interests**.

children.label: A.O. Hume and the Indian National Union
children.desc:
**A.O. Hume** was a retired British **civil servant**. He wanted an all-India body to point out the government's faults and suggest fixes.

- He wrote an **open letter** to graduates of **Calcutta University**, asking them to serve the people.
- In **1884**, with Indian leaders, he set up the **Indian National Union**.
- At its first meeting, on **Dadabhai Naoroji's** suggestion, the name changed to the **Indian National Congress**.

faq.q: Your turn: what was the Congress called before, and who renamed it?
faq.a: The **Indian National Union**. **Dadabhai Naoroji** suggested the new name.

children.label: The first session: Bombay, 1885
children.desc:
- The meeting was planned for **Pune**, but **plague** broke out there.
- It met at **Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College, Bombay (Mumbai)**, from **28 to 31 December 1885**.
- **72 delegates** came. The president was **W.C. Bonnerjee**.
- The **second session** was at **Calcutta (Kolkata)** in **1886**, under **Dadabhai Naoroji**.

**Why did the Viceroy, Lord Dufferin, favour it?** He hoped it would be a **'safety valve'**: a safe outlet for Indian anger, so it would **not explode** into another 1857.

faq.q: Your turn: where and under whom was the second session held?
faq.a: At **Calcutta (Kolkata)**, in 1886, under **Dadabhai Naoroji**.

children.label: The aims of the Congress

faq.q: Your turn: state three aims of the Congress.
faq.a: To build **national unity** beyond caste, religion and province; to **present popular demands** to the government; to **train public opinion**.

children.label: Quick check: associations and the Congress
children.desc:
Three questions on this milestone. Click an answer to check it.

Wrong? Read the reason, then look back at the step it names.

quiz.q: Who founded the East India Association, and where?
quiz.why: **Naoroji** worked in London to inform the British public. See *East India Association: Dadabhai Naoroji in London*.

quiz.q: Who presided over the first session of the Indian National Congress?
quiz.why: Naoroji presided over the **second** session (1886). Hume was the **founder**. See *The first session: Bombay, 1885*.

quiz.q: Why did Lord Dufferin favour the Congress?
options: He wanted to divide Hindus and Muslims
He wanted to end the Indian Association
He wanted a 'safety valve' for Indian discontent
He wanted India to be free
quiz.why: A safe outlet so anger **did not explode**. See *The first session: Bombay, 1885*.

topics.label: Exam toolkit: words and reasons
topics.desc: **Goal:** collect the easy marks: key terms, answers in the right shape, 'why' questions and dates.

children.label: Key terms to learn word for word
children.desc:
- **Nationalism:** a feeling of oneness among people who share a land, history and culture, and see themselves as one nation.
- **Vernacular Press Act (1878):** Lord Lytton's law forbidding Indian-language newspapers to print anything that roused dislike of the government.
- **Indian Arms Act (1878):** made it a crime for Indians to keep arms without a licence; it did not apply to the British.
- **Ilbert Bill (1883):** a bill to let Indian judges try Europeans; the government backed down after European protests.
- **Brahmo Samaj:** Rammohan Roy's society: one God, no idol worship, prayer and morality.
- **Satya Shodhak Samaj (1873):** Jyotiba Phule's society for social justice for the lower castes.
- **Safety valve:** Lord Dufferin's idea that the Congress would let out Indian discontent safely.

faq.q: Your turn: cover the list. What was the Vernacular Press Act?
faq.a: **Lord Lytton's** law of 1878 that stopped **Indian-language newspapers** from printing anything that roused **dislike of the government**.

children.label: Answers in the right shape
children.desc:
**Short answer (2 marks):** two points, each with **one fact**.

**Structured part (3 or 4 marks):** one point per mark. Start each point on a **new line**. Keep each to **one or two sentences**.

**Model answer.** *Explain the role of Dadabhai Naoroji in the growth of nationalism. (3 marks)*

- He founded the **East India Association** in **London** (1866) to tell the British public about India's problems.
- He suggested the name **Indian National Congress** for the Indian National Union.
- He presided over the **second session** of the Congress at **Calcutta** (1886).

**Three things that lose marks:** mixing up **Naoroji** (East India Association) and **Banerjee** (Indian Association); saying **Hume** was the first president; writing about 'the British' without naming **Lytton** or a law.

faq.q: Your turn: write a 2-mark answer. 'Who founded the Congress, and where was its first session?'
faq.a: It was founded by **A.O. Hume**. The first session was in **Bombay**, in December 1885, under **W.C. Bonnerjee**.

children.label: 'Why' questions: model answers
children.desc: Try each one in your notebook before you open it.

faq.q: Why is economic exploitation called the most important factor?
faq.a: It hurt **every class** (peasants, artisans, workers, educated), so they all saw **one common enemy**.

faq.q: Why did English newspapers escape the Vernacular Press Act?
faq.a: The Act targeted **Indian-language** papers, which reached **ordinary people**. English papers were read by few and many were British-owned.

faq.q: Why did the Ilbert Bill row help nationalism?
faq.a: Indians saw there was **no justice** where European interests were involved, and learned that **organised protest** gets results.

faq.q: Why were the early associations not enough?
faq.a: They were **local or regional**. India needed **one all-India** body.

faq.q: Why was the first session held in Bombay, not Pune?
faq.a: **Plague** had broken out in Pune.

children.label: Dates to learn
children.desc:
Read it top to bottom. Say each line aloud once.

- **1828:** Rammohan Roy founds the Brahmo Sabha (Brahmo Samaj).
- **1829:** Sati banned by Lord William Bentinck.
- **1838:** Landholders' Society, Calcutta.
- **1866:** East India Association, London (Naoroji).
- **1873:** Satya Shodhak Samaj (Phule).
- **1876:** Indian Association (Banerjee).
- **1877:** Delhi Durbar (Lytton).
- **1878:** Vernacular Press Act and Arms Act.
- **1882:** Press Act repealed (Ripon).
- **1883:** Ilbert Bill; Indian National Conference.
- **1884:** Indian National Union (Hume).
- **December 1885:** First Congress session, Bombay (Bonnerjee).
- **1886:** Second session, Calcutta (Naoroji).

faq.q: Your turn: which came first, the Indian Association or the Congress?
faq.a: The **Indian Association** (1876), nine years before the **Congress** (1885).

children.label: Picture study: who is this?
children.desc:
The exam may show a **picture** and ask who it is. Then it asks two or three facts. For each person, learn **who** and **two facts**.

- **Raja Rammohan Roy:** founded the **Brahmo Samaj**; fought **sati**; papers *Samvad Kaumudi* and *Mirat-ul-Akhbar*.
- **Jyotiba Phule:** schools for **girls** and **untouchables**; *Ghulamgiri*; **Satya Shodhak Samaj**.
- **Lord Lytton:** Delhi Durbar (1877); Vernacular Press Act and Arms Act (1878).
- **Dadabhai Naoroji:** **East India Association**, London; named the Congress; second session president.
- **Surendranath Banerjee:** **Indian Association**; Indian National Conference.
- **A.O. Hume:** retired civil servant who **founded the Congress**.
- **W.C. Bonnerjee:** **first president** of the Congress, Bombay, 1885.

faq.q: Your turn: a picture of Rammohan Roy. Name his organisation and two of its beliefs.
faq.a: The **Brahmo Samaj**. It believed in **one God** and **opposed idol worship**.

topics.label: Wrap up: last-minute revision and self-test
topics.desc: **Goal:** see the whole chapter on one page, then test yourself. Read the sheet the night before the exam and again on the morning.

children.label: Last-minute revision sheet
children.desc:
**The one idea:** nationalism grew from **pain, voice and platform**. British rule caused **common pain** (exploitation, harsh laws). Reformers and the press gave Indians **a voice**. Associations, then the **Congress (1885)**, gave them **a platform**.

**Dates to know**
- **1828** Brahmo Sabha (Roy). **1873** Satya Shodhak Samaj (Phule).
- **1866** East India Association (Naoroji, London). **1876** Indian Association (Banerjee).
- **1877** Delhi Durbar. **1878** Vernacular Press Act and Arms Act (Lytton). **1882** Press Act repealed (Ripon). **1883** Ilbert Bill.
- **1885** Congress founded at **Bombay**, 72 delegates, president **W.C. Bonnerjee**. **1886** second session at **Calcutta**, president **Dadabhai Naoroji**.

**Key terms**
- **Nationalism:** a feeling of oneness among people who share a land, history and culture, and see themselves as one nation.
- **Vernacular Press Act:** Lytton's law (1878) to gag newspapers in **Indian languages**.
- **Arms Act:** Indians needed a **licence** to keep arms; Europeans did not.
- **Ilbert Bill:** let **Indian judges** try Europeans; the government **backed down** after European protest.
- **Safety valve:** Dufferin's idea that the Congress would let off Indian anger **safely**.

**Key points**
- **Economic:** peasants (land revenue), artisans (ruined crafts), workers (factory owners), educated (no jobs). All felt it was **one enemy**.
- **Repressive (Lytton):** Durbar in a famine; Press Act; Arms Act; ICS age cut from **21 to 19**; cotton duties removed.
- **Rammohan Roy:** **Brahmo Samaj**; one God; against sati, child marriage, purdah; papers *Samvad Kaumudi* and *Mirat-ul-Akhbar*; 'father of the Indian Renaissance'.
- **Jyotiba Phule:** schools for **girls** and **untouchables** with **Savitribai**; *Ghulamgiri*; **Satya Shodhak Samaj**.
- **Press:** spread ideas, criticised the government, linked regions, told Indians about the world.
- **Congress aims:** friendship among workers; **national unity** beyond caste, religion and province; **present demands**; **train public opinion**.

**Traps:** **Lytton** passed the Press Act, **Ripon** repealed it. **Hume** founded the Congress; **Bonnerjee** was its first president; **Naoroji** the second, and he **named** it. It met in **Bombay**, not Pune (plague). Naoroji = **East India** Association; Banerjee = **Indian** Association.

children.label: Self-test (10 questions)
children.desc:
Ten questions from the whole chapter. Click an answer: it tells you if you are right, and why.

- **8 or more right:** you are ready for the textbook exercises.
- **Fewer than 8:** read the reasons, look back at the steps they name, then press **Start again**.

quiz.q: Which feeling was missing among Indians before British rule?
options: Loyalty to India as one nation
quiz.why: Loyalty was to a **king or kingdom**. See *Why India was not one nation before*.

quiz.q: Which group was a new class created by modern industry?
quiz.why: Factories created **workers**. See *Workers and the educated*.

quiz.q: The maximum age for the ICS exam was cut from 21 to:
quiz.why: A **younger** age made it harder for Indians, who had to travel to London. See *Lytton's other blows: the ICS age and cotton duties*.

quiz.q: Who repealed the Vernacular Press Act?
quiz.why: **Ripon**, in 1882. See *Two laws of 1878: the Press Act and the Arms Act*.

quiz.q: Rammohan Roy is called:
options: the father of the Indian Association
the Grand Old Man of India
the father of the Indian Renaissance
quiz.why: The **Grand Old Man** is Naoroji. See *Raja Rammohan Roy: one God, no sati*.

quiz.q: Jyotiba Phule founded:
quiz.why: In 1873, for **justice for lower castes**. See *Jyotiba Phule: education and equality*.

quiz.q: Who led the Indian Association?
quiz.why: Founded 1876. See *Indian Association: Surendranath Banerjee*.

quiz.q: Why was the first Congress session moved from Pune?
quiz.why: **Plague.** It met in **Bombay**. See *The first session: Bombay, 1885*.

quiz.q: Who suggested the name 'Indian National Congress'?
quiz.why: It was the **Indian National Union** until Naoroji's suggestion. See *A.O. Hume and the Indian National Union*.

quiz.q: Which was an aim of the early Congress?
options: To build national unity beyond caste, religion and province
To end British rule at once
quiz.why: Early aims were **moderate**. See *The aims of the Congress*.

topics.label: When you're ready: challenge questions
topics.desc: **For later.** These are like the harder questions at the end of the chapter. It is completely fine to skip this milestone the first time through.

children.label: Structured question: four factors
children.desc:
A structured question in three parts. Write your answer first, then open the box.

- (a) How did economic exploitation help nationalism grow? (3 marks)
- (b) Name two repressive measures of Lord Lytton. (3 marks)
- (c) Give two ways the press built national feeling. (4 marks)

faq.q: Model answer
faq.a:
(a) **Peasants** paid heavy land revenue; **artisans** lost work to British goods; **educated Indians** found no jobs. All saw **one enemy**.

(b) The **Vernacular Press Act** (1878); the **Indian Arms Act** (1878). (Also: the Delhi Durbar during a famine; the ICS age cut.)

(c) It **criticised** British policies daily; it let people in **different regions** share views and organise; it spread ideas of **liberty and equality**.

children.label: Structured question: the Congress is born
children.desc:
A structured question in three parts. Write your answer first, then open the box.

- (a) What was the Congress first called? Who renamed it? Who founded it? (3 marks)
- (b) Why did Lord Dufferin favour it? (3 marks)
- (c) Name two associations that came before it. (4 marks)

faq.q: Model answer
faq.a:
(a) The **Indian National Union**. **Dadabhai Naoroji** renamed it. **A.O. Hume** founded it.

(b) He hoped it would act as a **safety valve**, letting out Indian discontent **safely** instead of in a revolt.

(c) The **East India Association** (Naoroji, London, 1866) and the **Indian Association** (Banerjee, 1876).

topics.label: For teachers and parents
topics.desc:
**For the adults helping.** Students can skip this milestone.

The syllabus asks for four factors, two reformers, two associations and the first two sessions. The roadmap hangs them on **pain, voice and platform**.

children.label: How to help a student who is struggling
children.desc:
- Start with the question: 'What makes strangers feel like one team?' Then map the answers onto **pain, voice, platform**.
- Keep a **name-and-organisation** chart: Roy (Brahmo Samaj), Phule (Satya Shodhak Samaj), Naoroji (East India Association), Banerjee (Indian Association), Hume (Congress).
- Insist on **one fact per point**: a name, a date or a law.
- Pair the **Viceroys** with their acts: Lytton (Durbar, Press Act, Arms Act), Ripon (repeal, Ilbert Bill), Dufferin (safety valve).
- Use a newspaper activity: students write a short 1878 Indian-language headline that Lytton's Act would ban.
- Don't let students say the early Congress **demanded freedom**: its first aims were moderate.

children.label: A 6-period plan, with activities
children.desc:
- **Period 1:** What nationalism means; why India was not one nation; pain, voice and platform. Activity: 'from my king to my country'.
- **Period 2:** Economic exploitation of each class. Exercise I on exploitation.
- **Period 3:** Lytton's measures and the Ilbert Bill. Activity: write a banned headline. Exercise I on the Press Act.
- **Period 4:** Rammohan Roy and Jyotiba Phule; how reform built nationalism. Exercise III (picture study).
- **Period 5:** The press; the early associations; Naoroji and Banerjee.
- **Period 6:** Hume, the first two sessions, the aims; revision sheet, self-test and exit ticket. Exercise II.

children.label: Mistakes to watch for
children.desc:
- Saying **Ripon** passed the Press Act (he **repealed** it).
- Giving **Hume** as the first **president** (it was **W.C. Bonnerjee**).
- Placing the first session at **Pune** (it moved to **Bombay**).
- Swapping **Naoroji's** and **Banerjee's** associations.
- Writing that the early Congress wanted **independence**.
- Listing factors with **no examples**.

children.label: Exit ticket (5 minutes)
children.desc: Five short questions covering the main ideas. The answers are below.

faq.q: 1. What is nationalism?
faq.a: A feeling of **oneness** among people who see themselves as **one nation**.

faq.q: 2. Name two of Lytton's repressive measures.
faq.a: The **Vernacular Press Act** and the **Arms Act** (1878).

faq.q: 3. Which society did Rammohan Roy found?
faq.a: The **Brahmo Samaj**.

faq.q: 4. Who led the Indian Association?
faq.a: **Surendranath Banerjee**.

faq.q: 5. Where and under whom was the first Congress session?
faq.a: **Bombay**, 1885, under **W.C. Bonnerjee**.
